explanations.explanation: Verse 1 says Sanballat was “furious and filled with indignation.” Sanballat, the man who already mocked this plan once, hears the wall is really going up and he does not take it well. I think his whole day just got ruined. Nothing sours a man like somebody else's progress.

Not quite, friend. The text says Sanballat was “furious and filled with indignation.” A thrilled man doesn't go ridiculing the Jews, and that's exactly what he does next. Nobody is passing out party hats in Samaria.

The text never calls Sanballat frightened. It says he was “furious and filled with indignation,” and then he ridiculed the Jews. So what we see from him is anger and mockery. Anything else would be me adding to the story.

That's the heart of it. Sanballat asks, “Can they restore the wall by themselves?” and then, “Can they bring these burnt stones back to life from the mounds of rubble?” I think every question is a sneer that says this job is too big for them. It's a whole speech dressed up as a pile of questions.

explanations.answer: They're building in the wrong place
explanations.explanation: Look at his questions again. Not one of them says anything about where the wall is going. He asks if they can restore it, if they can finish it, and if they can bring burnt stones back to life. I think he's mocking whether they can finish, not where they build.

He actually points the other way. Sanballat asks, “Will they complete it in a day?” and I think he's poking fun at how weak he thinks the builders are. He calls them “feeble” in verse 2. A man worried about speed wouldn't use that word.

Yes, and Tobiah the Ammonite, standing beside Sanballat, is the one who says it. In his words: “If even a fox were to climb up on what they are building, it would break down their wall of stones!” That's the whole joke, and he seems proud of it. Not exactly comedy-special material, but he got it out.

This one is actually true, friend. Tobiah the Ammonite, who stood beside Sanballat, says, “If even a fox were to climb up on what they are building, it would break down their wall of stones!” The fox is right there in verse 3. It's an easy one to doubt because it sounds so silly.

explanations.answer: Turn it back on their own heads
explanations.explanation: That's his prayer in verse 4: “Turn their scorn back upon their own heads…” Nehemiah, who is leading the rebuilding, brings the mockery straight to God instead of answering it himself. He starts the prayer with “Hear us, O God, for we are despised.” He says it plainly.

Nehemiah doesn't ask for that. His prayer says, “Turn their scorn back upon their own heads…” He asks God to send the scorn back where it came from, not to wipe it from the builders' memory. Forgetting never comes up.

explanations.answer: Make the builders stronger through it
explanations.explanation: That's a nice thought, but it isn't what he prays. In verse 4 Nehemiah says, “Turn their scorn back upon their own heads…” The prayer is about the scorn going back to the ones who threw it. Nothing in it mentions making anyone stronger.

It's the opposite, friend. Nehemiah prays, “Do not cover up their iniquity or let their sin be blotted out from Your sight…” He asks God not to blot it out. It's a hard prayer to read, and it's his own.

Right, he asks for the opposite. Verse 5 says, “Do not cover up their iniquity or let their sin be blotted out from Your sight…” So he asks God not to let it be blotted out. It's a hard prayer, and it comes straight from Nehemiah.
That's the reason he gives. Verse 5 says, “…for they have provoked the builders.” The ones doing the hammering and hauling are the ones taking the heat. Nehemiah brings that hurt straight to God.
Close to the temple crowd, but no. The text says, “…for they have provoked the builders.” The mockery is aimed at the people working on the wall. Priests aren't named in this verse.
The king isn't in this prayer at all. Verse 5 says, “…for they have provoked the builders.” That's the group Nehemiah names, the ones working on the wall. Nobody in verse 5 is wearing a crown.

Verse 6 says they rebuilt the wall “until all of it was joined together up to half its height.” That means the whole wall is connected and halfway up. That's a lot of progress with a crowd of mockers watching. Halfway up is still a long way from done, and I think they know it.

explanations.answer: All the way to the top
explanations.explanation: Not yet. The text says the wall was joined together “up to half its height.” The top is still ahead of them. Halfway is real progress, though.
They've done much more than that. Verse 6 says the whole wall was joined together “up to half its height.” That's way past just getting started. Sanballat's fox would have a harder climb by now.

explanations.answer: The people had a mind to work
explanations.explanation: That's the reason verse 6 gives: “for the people had a mind to work.” No hired help or bonus is mentioned. They wanted to do it, and the wall kept rising. I'd take a team like that over any shiny new equipment.
The text never says that. Verse 6 gives the reason as, “for the people had a mind to work.” The workers were the people already there. No extra crew shows up in this passage.
No wages come up in this passage. The reason given in verse 6 is, “for the people had a mind to work.” Their own heart for the job kept them going.

explanations.answer: To come and fight against Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: That's it. Verse 8 says all of them “conspired to come and fight against Jerusalem and create a hindrance.” Sanballat and Tobiah are joined by the Arabs, Ammonites and Ashdodites. The mocking has turned into a plan.

explanations.answer: To offer to help finish the wall
explanations.explanation: Nobody in this crowd offers a hammer. Verse 8 says they “conspired to come and fight against Jerusalem and create a hindrance.” They're furious, and the plan is a fight.

explanations.answer: To send a complaint to the king
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention any complaint letter here. Verse 8 says they “conspired to come and fight against Jerusalem and create a hindrance.” It's a plot to come in person.
Verse 9 says, “So we prayed to our God…” The very first thing they do about the threat is pray. Nehemiah tells it right in the same breath as the guard. Prayer comes first and it doesn't get skipped.
Yes, verse 9 says they “posted a guard against them day and night.” They pray, and they also put someone on watch. Both are in the same verse.
Nobody runs in verse 9. It says, “So we prayed to our God and posted a guard against them day and night.” The builders pray and stay at their posts. Running isn't in the plan.
No letter gets sent in this verse. Verse 9 says they prayed and posted a guard against the enemies. Nehemiah is dealing with this face to face, not by mail.
A gate is a fine thing, but verse 9 doesn't post one. It says they “posted a guard against them day and night.” What they post is a person.
The text says otherwise. Verse 9 says they posted a guard “day and night.” That means the watch never clocked out. Nobody gets to stop watching when the sun goes down.
Right, the guard isn't a daytime-only job. Verse 9 says they posted a guard against the enemies “day and night.” That's around the clock. Somebody is always awake.

explanations.answer: There's too much rubble to ever finish
explanations.explanation: That's what they say in verse 10: “The strength of the laborer fails, and there is so much rubble that we will never be able to rebuild the wall.” The voices of doubt are now coming from the people of Judah, not just the enemies. I think that stings more. Plenty of us have looked at a huge pile of work and said the same thing.

explanations.answer: The wall is nearly finished now
explanations.explanation: That's not what they say. In verse 10 the people of Judah say, “…there is so much rubble that we will never be able to rebuild the wall.” They're looking at the mess, not at the finish line.

explanations.answer: The enemies have finally given up
explanations.explanation: The enemies haven't given up at all. In verse 11 they say, “…we will come into their midst, kill them, and put an end to the work.” The people of Judah are talking about rubble and tired arms in verse 10.

explanations.answer: Before the builders know or see a thing
explanations.explanation: That's their plan in verse 11: “Before they know or see a thing, we will come into their midst, kill them, and put an end to the work.” It's meant to be a surprise attack. This part of the story is heavy, and the threat is serious.

explanations.answer: Right after they send a warning
explanations.explanation: There's no warning in their plan. The enemies say, “Before they know or see a thing, we will come into their midst…” The whole point is that the builders see it coming too late.

explanations.answer: Once the wall is all finished
explanations.explanation: They don't plan to wait that long. Verse 11 says, “Before they know or see a thing, we will come into their midst, kill them, and put an end to the work.” They want to stop the work, so the wall wouldn't be finished.
Verse 12 says the Jews who lived nearby “told us ten times over.” Ten! That's a whole lot of the same message. I think Nehemiah heard it loud and clear.
It's way more than two. Verse 12 says the Jews who lived nearby “told us ten times over.” That's a lot of warnings.
Seven is a good number, but the text says more. Verse 12 says they “told us ten times over.” Ten is the number.

explanations.answer: Behind the lowest sections of the wall
explanations.explanation: Verse 13 says, “So I stationed men behind the lowest sections of the wall, at the vulnerable areas.” Nehemiah puts people where the wall is weakest. That's the spot to guard, and he knew it.

explanations.answer: On top of the tallest towers
explanations.explanation: No towers show up in this verse. Nehemiah says he stationed men “behind the lowest sections of the wall, at the vulnerable areas.” He's putting people at the low spots.
The text puts them somewhere else. Verse 13 says Nehemiah stationed men “behind the lowest sections of the wall, at the vulnerable areas.” They're behind the wall, not out past the gates.
The text says the opposite. Verse 13 says Nehemiah stationed the men “by families.” So they stood with their families, not away from them. Nobody gets sent off alone.
Yes, he keeps families together. Verse 13 says, “I stationed them by families with their swords, spears, and bows.” They stand with their families. I think that makes the posts mean a lot more.
That's how he starts. Nehemiah stands up and says, “Do not be afraid of them.” Then he tells them where to look: “Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome…” Fear gets answered with remembering.
Close, but that's not the word. Nehemiah says, “Do not be afraid of them.” The enemies had been mocking, but his speech is about fear.
Jealousy isn't in this speech. Nehemiah says, “Do not be afraid of them.” He's talking to the nobles, the officials and the rest of the people about the threat.
That's his list in verse 14: “…fight for your brothers, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your homes.” He's naming the people and the places they love. That's a lot to stand up for.

explanations.answer: The king of Persia and his throne
explanations.explanation: The king isn't in this speech. Nehemiah says, “…fight for your brothers, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your homes.” He points them to family and home.

explanations.answer: Their own honor and their good name
explanations.explanation: Honor never comes up. Verse 14 says, “…fight for your brothers, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your homes.” He points them to the people and places close to them.
Yes, verse 15 says the enemies heard “that we were aware of their scheme and that God had frustrated it.” Nehemiah gives God the credit for it. The plan didn't go through.
It's true, friend. Verse 15 says the enemies heard “that we were aware of their scheme and that God had frustrated it.” Nehemiah says it right there. The credit goes to God.

explanations.answer: Goes back to his own work on the wall
explanations.explanation: Verse 15 says, “…each of us returned to his own work on the wall.” Back to the stones and the mortar. The scare doesn't send them home.

explanations.answer: Marches out to attack the enemies
explanations.explanation: Nobody marches out. Verse 15 says, “…each of us returned to his own work on the wall.” They go back to building.
They stay put. Verse 15 says, “…each of us returned to his own work on the wall.” The work goes on in Jerusalem.
Verse 16 says, “…half of my servants did the work…” So half keep building. The wall still has to get built.
That's the other half. Verse 16 says they “held spears, shields, bows, and armor.” One half builds and the other half guards.
Stones are what the builders work with, but that's not the word in the verse. It says half did “the work” while the other half held spears. The stones themselves aren't named there.
No scrolls here. Verse 16 says half of Nehemiah's servants did the work while the other half held “spears, shields, bows, and armor.” It's a building and guarding crew.
Prayer is a big part of this chapter, like in verse 9. But verse 16 says the other half held “spears, shields, bows, and armor.” Those are the things in their hands.
It's the opposite. Verse 18 says, “each of the builders worked with his sword strapped at his side.” The sword goes to work with him.
Yes, no swords stay home. Verse 18 says, “And each of the builders worked with his sword strapped at his side.” They build and stay ready.

That's the plan. Nehemiah says, “Wherever you hear the sound of the horn, rally to us there.” The builders are spread out far along the wall, so the horn tells them where to gather. It's a simple signal for a big job.

explanations.answer: Run back to their own homes
explanations.explanation: That's not what the horn means. Nehemiah says, “Wherever you hear the sound of the horn, rally to us there.” The horn calls them toward the trouble, not away.

explanations.answer: Climb to the top of the wall
explanations.explanation: The wall is only half its height, and the text doesn't send them up it. Nehemiah says, “Wherever you hear the sound of the horn, rally to us there.” They gather where the sound is.
Yes, verse 20 ends with, “Our God will fight for us!” Nehemiah says it right after telling them about the horn. The people hear it from him.
It's true. Nehemiah says in verse 20, “Our God will fight for us!” That's how he finishes his instructions about the horn.

explanations.answer: From dawn until the stars came out
explanations.explanation: Verse 21 says they kept going “from the break of dawn until the stars came out.” That's a full day of work, and half the men are holding spears the whole time. I'd need a nap just reading it.
It runs much longer than that. Verse 21 says “from the break of dawn until the stars came out.” They keep at it all the way to evening.

explanations.answer: Only through the dark of night
explanations.explanation: Verse 21 says they worked “from the break of dawn until the stars came out.” So it starts in the morning and runs into the evening. The night guard is a separate thing in verse 22.
Verse 22 has Nehemiah say, “Let every man and his servant spend the night inside Jerusalem…” They stay in the city. That keeps everyone close to the wall.
Samaria is where Sanballat's army comes from (Nehemiah 4:2). Nehemiah wants his people staying in Jerusalem. Verse 22 says, “Let every man and his servant spend the night inside Jerusalem…”
Jericho isn't in this verse. Nehemiah says, “Let every man and his servant spend the night inside Jerusalem…” They stay right in the city.

explanations.answer: To stand guard by night and work by day
explanations.explanation: That's his reason in verse 22: “…so that they can stand guard by night and work by day.” So the guard goes on in the dark and the building goes on in the light. Pretty much no days off.

explanations.answer: To rest up well before the next day
explanations.explanation: Nehemiah's stated reason is a different one. Verse 22 says, “…so that they can stand guard by night and work by day.” They're in the city to guard it overnight.

explanations.answer: To keep the enemies from finding their homes
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give that reason. Verse 22 says, “…so that they can stand guard by night and work by day.” The point is guard duty at night and work by day.
Yes, verse 23 says, “neither I nor my brothers nor my servants nor the guards with me changed out of our clothes…” Nehemiah is in this with everyone else. That's one long stretch in the same outfit.
It's true, friend. Verse 23 says, “neither I nor my brothers nor my servants nor the guards with me changed out of our clothes…” Nehemiah says it about himself and his crew.
Verse 23 ends, “…each carried his weapon, even to go for water.” Even a simple trip for water means a weapon in the hand. That's how alert they stay.
No market in this verse. It says, “…each carried his weapon, even to go for water.” The water run is the ordinary errand they mention.
The temple isn't mentioned. Verse 23 says, “…each carried his weapon, even to go for water.” That's the everyday trip with a weapon along.
